title: Chord Progressions
intro: Chords give a melody its colour and direction. Songwriters mostly use a handful of progressions, varied by key, rhythm, inversion and a few borrowed chords; knowing why they work lets you choose and change them on purpose.

blocks.text: Every key offers three kinds of chord: tonic (I, vi; home), predominant (IV, ii; moving away) and dominant (V; pulling home). A progression that moves tonic → predominant → dominant → tonic sounds purposeful (see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)). In C major: C, Am | F, Dm | G | C.

items: I–IV–V–I and I–IV–I–V: folk, country, early rock, the blues.
I–V–vi–IV (C–G–Am–F) and its rotation vi–IV–I–V: countless modern pop songs. Starting on vi makes the same chords sound minor and wistful.
ii–V–I: the jazz cadence, also common in soul and R&B, often as ii7–V7–Imaj7.
i–♭VI–♭III–♭VII (Am–F–C–G): the minor-key loop; the same chords as I–V–vi–IV in a different order.
I–♭VII–IV–I (D–C–G–D): rock's Mixolydian progression (♭VII is the major chord on the flattened seventh, found in Mixolydian and in the parallel minor).

blocks.text: To find chords for a melody you already have: for each bar, list the long or strongly placed melody notes and pick a chord that contains them. In C, a bar that sits on E and G suggests C or Em; a bar on F and A suggests F or Dm. Then check the chain of chords for good function, and prefer chords that change at bar lines. When two choices fit, the one with a stronger bass line usually wins.

items: Seventh and added-note chords: Cmaj7 for a softer tonic, Am7 or Fadd9 for warmth, Gsus4 → G to delay the dominant (see Extended and Altered Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords/extended-and-altered)).
Borrowed chords from the parallel minor: iv (Fm in C) after IV for a bittersweet turn, ♭VI–♭VII–I for a triumphant ending (see Chromatic Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/chromatic-harmony)).
Secondary dominants: E7 before Am, A7 before Dm, D7 before G, for a stronger pull to the next chord (see Secondary Dominants (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/secondary-dominants)).
Inversions and pedal points: keep the bass on one note (C/E, F/C, G/B) or walk it stepwise, C–C/B–Am–Am/G, which adds motion without changing the chord set.

blocks.title: Harmonise
blocks.text: A melody in G major holds B and D in one bar, and A and C in the next, then G. Suggest chords.
solution: G major's chords: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F♯°. B and D fit G (G B D) or Bm (B D F♯). A and C fit Am (A C E) or D7 (D F♯ A C). A strong choice: G | D7 | G (I–V7–I); a softer one: G | Am | G.
blocks.answer: For example G | D7 | G or G | Am | G
